title: Triple treble
subtitle: UK trtr — the tallest standard stitch
excerpt: The triple treble (UK trtr, US dtr) is the tallest stitch in everyday crochet use. Three initial yarn overs, four pull-through steps, a chain-5 turning chain. This tutorial covers the move and the situations where such height is genuinely useful.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), lace and openwork chapter (Project Gutenberg #20776). Weldon's Practical Crochet, Volume 5.
heroPrompt: Tall triple treble stitches in cream cotton DK, showing the very open airy columns and the multiple twist marks on each stitch shaft, natural background.

glossaryTerms.definition: The tallest standard crochet stitch. Made with three initial yarn overs and four pull-through steps. UK triple treble equals US double treble (dtr). Appears in extended lace patterns and tall decorative borders.

content.text: extends the tall-stitch logic one step beyond the double treble. Three initial yarn overs load the hook; the stitch then works off in four pull-through steps. The result is a very tall, open column useful in lace borders, spike stitches, and any pattern where the stitch needs to reach back several rows.
Yarn over three times before inserting the hook.
Insert the hook under both top loops of the next stitch (or into a chain space, or two rows below, as the pattern requires).
Yarn over, pull through the stitch. Five loops on the hook.
Yarn over, pull through two loops. Four remain.
Yarn over, pull through two loops. Three remain.
Yarn over, pull through two loops. Two remain.
Yarn over, pull through the last two loops. One loop. The triple treble is complete.
The turning chain for triple treble rows is ch 5, which counts as the first triple treble.
When to use the triple treble

Triple trebles appear in lace patterns where a very open mesh is needed, in spike stitches that reach two or three rows back to create a vertical colour accent, and in tall fan or shell patterns where the extra height opens the fan dramatically. They are less common than treble or double treble but the move is the same logic and the stitch is easy to identify: five loops on the hook after inserting is the triple treble signature.

attrs.heading: Triple treble problems
attrs.intro: Two problems that are specific to triple trebles.

items.symptom: The three initial yarn overs collapse and tangle before inserting
items.cause: The yarn overs were worked too loosely and overlap each other.
items.fix: Work each yarn over snugly and hold them in order with a light finger pressure while inserting. Take them slowly until the muscle memory is established.

items.symptom: The stitch count on the loops remaining is lost partway through
items.cause: Working too fast across multiple pull-through steps.
items.fix: Count the loops before each pull-through: 5, 4, 3, 2, 1. A spoken count takes two seconds per stitch and eliminates this error entirely.

content.text: From the triple treble, the natural next pattern is a spike stitch: a triple treble worked two or three rows below the current row (skipping the stitches above the insertion point) to pull a long column of colour through the piece. This is the mechanism behind many textured striped patterns.
